hints: Notice the question gives mass $m$ and momenta $p_1$ and $p_2$, so rewrite velocity as $v = p/m$ to link momentum to kinetic energy.
Recall $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ becomes $E_k = p^2/2m$ after substituting for $v$, so find $E_{k1}$ and $E_{k2}$ separately.
Subtract initial from final $E_{k2} - E_{k1}$ and check why $(p_2^2 - p_1^2)$ is different from $(p_2 - p_1)^2$.
walkthrough: Write momentum as $p = mv$, so velocity is $v = p/m$ for the same car of mass $m$.
Substitute into kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(p/m)^2$, giving the useful rule $E_k = p^2/2m$.
Apply to the two states: initial $E_{k1} = p_1^2/2m$ and final $E_{k2} = p_2^2/2m$.
Increase in kinetic energy is final minus initial: $\Delta E_k = p_2^2/2m - p_1^2/2m = (p_2^2 - p_1^2)/2m$.
This has units of $\text{J}$ and is positive for $p_2 > p_1$. This is option A.

options.A: Final kinetic minus initial kinetic gives $(p_2^2 - p_1^2)/2m$, which is positive since $p_2 > p_1$.
options.B: This squares the change in momentum, but kinetic energy depends on $p^2$, so you must subtract the squares, not square the subtraction.
options.C: This is linear in $p$ and has wrong units for energy, since kinetic energy varies as momentum squared.
options.D: This is linear in $p$ and negative for an increase, so it cannot represent the increase in kinetic energy.
